lessons.title: Using Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
lessons.eli5: Before you build a treehouse, you ask who will use it, how big it must be and what could go wrong. Claude is a very fast helper for that thinking: hand it your messy notes and it sorts them into a clear list of needs, open questions and guesses that still need checking. You still decide what gets built.
lessons.body:
## Why this matters

Many failed projects fail before anyone starts building: the team solved the wrong problem, or missed a need nobody wrote down. Task 4.1 tests whether you can use Claude to **turn messy input into clear requirements**, and to **judge which use cases are worth doing with Claude at all**. The exam frames this as business judgment, not feature trivia.

## From mess to structure

Requirements usually arrive scattered: a meeting transcript, five emails, a survey export, a manager's voice note. Claude is good at reading all of it at once and sorting it. Attach or paste the material, then ask for a specific structure.

| Raw input | Ask Claude to produce |
|---|---|
| Stakeholder interview notes | Needs grouped by stakeholder, with direct quotes as evidence |
| A long email thread | Decisions made, decisions still open, and who owns each |
| Survey free-text answers | Themes with counts and representative comments |
| A vague request ("make onboarding better") | Clarifying questions, assumptions and a draft problem statement |

A useful split to request every time:

- **Requirements**: what the solution must do ("new hires can find their equipment request form on day one").
- **Constraints**: limits it must respect (budget, deadline, policy, approved tools).
- **Assumptions**: things believed but not confirmed. These are the items most likely to sink the project.
- **Open questions**: what you need to ask a human before you go further.

Asking Claude to **label assumptions separately** is one of the highest-value moves here. A requirements list that mixes facts with guesses looks finished but isn't.

## Let Claude interview you

When the request is fuzzy, don't ask Claude to write the requirements straight away. Ask it to question you first:

> I need to plan a new process for handling customer refund requests. Before drafting anything, ask me up to 8 clarifying questions about volume, who approves refunds, current pain points and any policy limits. Ask them one group at a time.

This flips the usual flow. Claude surfaces the gaps (who approves? what's the dollar threshold?) that you would otherwise find out about late. Your answers then become the context for the draft.

## Stress-test the requirements

Once you have a draft, use Claude as a critic:

- "List edge cases this process doesn't handle."
- "Which of these requirements conflict with each other?"
- "Rewrite each requirement so someone could test whether it was met."
- "What would a finance reviewer object to? What would a frontline agent object to?"

Asking for different perspectives is cheap with Claude and catches blind spots. It is still a draft: **the stakeholders confirm the requirements**, not Claude. Claude has never met your customers and doesn't know your internal politics, unwritten rules or last year's failed attempt unless you tell it.

## Choosing good use cases for Claude

Part of 4.1 is analyzing **use cases**: which tasks should Claude help with? A simple scoring grid works well, and Claude can help you fill it in for a long list of candidate tasks.

| Factor | Favors Claude | Warns you off (or needs heavy controls) |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency | Happens weekly or daily | One-off, rare |
| Effort today | Time-consuming reading, drafting, summarizing | Already quick |
| Error impact | Mistakes are easy to catch and cheap to fix | Errors reach customers, regulators or affect people's jobs |
| Data sensitivity | Public or internal, non-personal data | Personal, health, financial or confidential data outside approved tools |
| Verifiability | A human can check the output quickly | No one can tell if it's right |
| Needs live systems | Works from documents you can provide | Needs real-time data or actions in other systems |

**Start with high-value, low-risk, repeatable tasks** that a human can review easily: meeting summaries, first drafts of standard documents, sorting feedback into themes. Leave high-stakes, hard-to-verify or highly sensitive tasks until you have controls and approvals in place.

## Worked example

An HR operations lead, Priya, wants to "use AI for onboarding". She pastes in anonymized notes from interviews with six managers and a list of current onboarding steps.

1. She asks Claude to group the managers' complaints into themes, with how many managers raised each one. Top themes: equipment arrives late, new hires can't find policies, managers repeat the same welcome talk.
2. She asks Claude to propose candidate use cases and score them with the grid above. Claude suggests (a) a policy Q&A Project built on the employee handbook, (b) personalized welcome-email drafts, and (c) automatically approving equipment orders.
3. She checks the scoring. (a) and (b) are frequent, easy to review and low risk. (c) needs a live connection to the purchasing system and changes spending decisions, so it is **not a prompt-level task**: she notes it for the IT and development team instead of trying to force it into a chat.
4. She asks Claude for the open questions on (a): who keeps the handbook current, and which policies differ by country?

The outcome is a short list of realistic starting points, a clear hand-off for the part that needs engineering, and questions to take back to people.

## What the exam looks for

The best answer usually **uses Claude to structure and challenge the thinking, then has humans validate it**. Watch for options that let Claude define requirements alone, skip stakeholder confirmation, or pick the flashiest use case over the safest, most repeatable one.
keyTakeaways: Claude turns scattered notes, emails and transcripts into structured requirements, constraints, assumptions and open questions.
Ask Claude to label assumptions separately from confirmed facts; hidden assumptions sink projects.
When a request is vague, have Claude ask you clarifying questions before it drafts anything.
Use Claude as a critic: edge cases, conflicts, testable wording and stakeholder perspectives.
Score use cases on frequency, effort, error impact, data sensitivity, verifiability and need for live systems; start with high-value, low-risk, repeatable tasks.
Stakeholders, not Claude, confirm the final requirements.
examTips: When asked how to start with a vague request, prefer "have Claude ask clarifying questions" or "give Claude the source notes" over "ask Claude to write the full requirements now".
For "which use case should the team pilot first?", choose the frequent, easy-to-verify, low-risk task, not the most ambitious one.
A use case that needs live system access or automatic actions in other tools points to a Developer or Architect hand-off.
If an option adds human or stakeholder validation of Claude's requirements draft, it is usually stronger than one that ships the draft as-is.
commonTraps: Treating Claude's requirements draft as final without checking it with the people who own the process.
Picking the use case with the biggest potential payoff even though errors would reach customers or regulators.
Expecting Claude to know internal context (past decisions, unwritten rules) it was never given.
Pasting raw interview notes containing personal data into an unapproved tool instead of anonymizing first.

lessons.title: Research, planning and process optimization with Claude
lessons.eli5: Think of Claude as a fast junior analyst. It can read lots of sources and come back with a cited summary, sketch a project plan, or point out where a process wastes time. Like any junior analyst, its work gets checked before the boss acts on it.
lessons.body:
## Three jobs, one habit

Task 4.2 bundles three related jobs: **researching** a question, **planning** work, and **optimizing** an existing process. The same habit runs through all three: Claude does the heavy first pass quickly, and a human checks the parts that matter before anyone acts.

## 1. Research

Pick the right feature for the depth of the question.

| Need | Best fit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Quick fact or explanation you can sanity-check | Regular chat (with web search on if it's about recent events) | Fast and cheap |
| Answer from your own documents | Attach the files, or use a Project that holds them | Claude works from your sources, not memory |
| Multi-source investigation with citations | **Research** | Claude runs several searches that build on each other and returns a cited report |

What the Help Center says about **Research**, at the time of writing:
- It is on **paid plans** (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise) and needs **web search turned on**.
- Claude works agentically, running searches that build on each other, and typically answers **in minutes**.
- It returns **citations** so you can check the findings, and it can also draw on connected Google Workspace content (Gmail, Calendar, Docs).
- Research sessions **use your usage limits faster** than ordinary chats.

**Citations are a starting point, not proof.** Open the key sources and confirm they say what the report claims, especially numbers, quotes, dates and anything you will repeat to a client or executive. A source can exist and still not support the sentence it's attached to.

Good research prompts give scope and criteria:

> Research how mid-sized logistics companies are handling returns for e-commerce clients. Focus on the last two years, prefer industry reports and company announcements over opinion blogs, and separate what is well-established from what is a single-source claim.

## 2. Planning

Claude drafts planning documents quickly once you supply the facts:

- project plans broken into phases, milestones and dependencies
- timelines with assumptions shown ("assumes legal review takes 5 working days")
- risk registers (risk, likelihood, impact, mitigation, owner)
- RACI charts (who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed)
- meeting agendas, communication plans and launch checklists

Two rules keep these honest. First, **give Claude the real constraints**: team size, deadlines, budget, approval steps. A plan built on invented constraints is fiction. Second, **a human validates it**. Claude doesn't know that your legal team is backed up for a month or that a key person is on leave. Ask Claude to list the assumptions behind the plan, then check them.

A useful pattern is plan-then-execute. Ask for an outline first, approve or adjust it, then ask for detail on one phase at a time. Each step is easier to check than one giant document.

## 3. Process optimization

To improve a process, Claude first needs to see it. Describe the current steps (or paste the procedure document) and ask Claude to:

1. **Map** the current flow step by step, with who does each step and how long it takes.
2. **Find friction**: waiting time, hand-offs, rework loops, copy-and-paste, steps that exist only for historical reasons.
3. **Classify** each step: keep as is, remove, simplify, or have Claude assist.
4. **Propose** a future-state flow and say what would need to be true for it to work.

| Step type | Typical Claude role |
|---|---|
| Reading and summarizing incoming material | Strong fit: Claude drafts, a human skims |
| Writing standard documents from a template | Strong fit: Claude drafts, a human edits |
| Sorting or tagging items by clear rules | Good fit, with spot checks |
| Approvals, commitments, decisions about people | Keep with a human |
| Moving data between systems automatically | Usually needs a Developer or Architect build |

## Worked example

A school's operations manager, Tom, spends two days each term building the exam timetable and sending notices to parents.

- **Research**: he uses Research to collect guidance on accessible exam arrangements, then opens the three most-cited sources to confirm the details before quoting them to staff.
- **Planning**: he gives Claude the room list, staff availability and exam dates and asks for a draft timetable plus a list of conflicts it could not resolve. He fixes the conflicts himself because he knows which teachers can swap.
- **Optimization**: he describes the current notice process. Claude points out that he rewrites the same parent letter for every year group. He saves a letter template in a Project, so future letters take minutes. Sending the letters automatically from the school system is flagged as an IT request, not something to do from chat.

## What the exam looks for

Expect questions where Claude gave a fast, plausible answer and you must choose the next step. The strong answer **verifies the key sources or assumptions in proportion to the stakes**. Weak answers either trust the output because it has citations, or throw the work away instead of checking it.
keyTakeaways: Match the research depth to the feature: chat for quick checks, attached files or a Project for your own material, Research for multi-source cited investigations.
Research (paid plans, web search on) runs searches that build on each other, cites sources, can use connected Google Workspace and uses limits faster.
Citations must be opened and checked; a real source may not support the claim attached to it.
Give Claude the real constraints when planning, ask it to list its assumptions, and have a human validate the plan.
For process optimization: map the current flow, find the friction, classify each step, then propose a future state.
Decisions, approvals and system-to-system automation stay with humans or go to technical teams.
examTips: If the scenario needs a cited, multi-source answer, Research is usually the feature to pick; if it needs answers from internal documents, attaching them or using a Project is better.
When Claude has produced a cited report for an important audience, the best next step is to verify the key citations, not to forward it or regenerate it.
For planning questions, favor options that supply real constraints and ask Claude to surface assumptions.
For process questions, the right first step is usually mapping the current process, not jumping to a new tool.
commonTraps: Treating the presence of citations as proof that every claim is correct.
Using Research for a simple question that a normal chat answers, wasting usage limits.
Accepting a project timeline built on constraints Claude made up.
Automating a step that contains a judgment call (an approval, a decision about a person) just because it is slow.

lessons.title: Supporting solution design, development and iteration
lessons.eli5: Claude lets you build a cardboard model of your idea in minutes: a draft document, a mock-up, a small clickable tool. You show it to people, learn what is wrong, and fix it the same afternoon. When the idea needs real plumbing (connecting to company systems), you bring in the builders.
lessons.body:
## Design by trying, not by guessing

Task 4.3 is about using Claude to help **design a solution, build a first version, and improve it based on feedback**. For a non-technical professional the key tool is the fast prototype: something concrete that people can react to. Reacting to a draft is much easier than describing something in the abstract.

## What you can prototype without code

| You want | Use | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A process document, policy draft, playbook or proposal | An **Artifact** (or a file) | Edit it in place, iterate, share |
| A slide outline or a deck | Artifact or file creation | Claude can create PowerPoint, Word, Excel and PDF files |
| A form, checklist, calculator or simple dashboard | An interactive **Artifact** | A small tool people can click through |
| A reusable assistant for a recurring task | A **Project** with instructions and knowledge files | The team uses the same setup every time |
| A repeatable method Claude should follow | A **Skill** (where your organization allows them) | Packaged instructions and resources Claude loads when relevant |

From the Help Center, at the time of writing: an Artifact is significant, self-contained content (typically over 15 lines) that you are likely to edit, reuse or share, such as documents, diagrams, dashboards and small interactive tools. Artifacts start **private** and can be published and shared, and an Artifact can even call Claude itself to become a small AI-powered app. Artifacts are available on all plans.

## The iteration loop

1. **Define what good looks like** before you build: who uses it, what problem it solves, how you will judge it. ("Store managers can complete the incident form in under three minutes on a phone.")
2. **Build a first version** with Claude. Ask for something small that works over something big that's half done.
3. **Test with real people and real examples.** Use three to five realistic cases, including an awkward one.
4. **Collect specific feedback**: what confused people, what was missing, what was wrong.
5. **Give targeted change requests**: "Keep the layout. Move the injury question to the top, and make the date field default to today." Targeted edits keep what already works. Blank-slate regeneration throws it away.
6. **Repeat**, keeping a short log of what changed and why.

Ask Claude for **options** at the design stage ("give me three different ways to structure this intake form, with pros and cons of each"). Comparing alternatives early is cheap, and changing direction late is expensive.

## Know where your role stops

The guide is explicit that Associates hand complex or technical builds to **Claude Developers and Architects**. A prototype that works in a chat is not a production system. Signs you have reached that boundary:

- it must read or write **live data in company systems** (CRM, HR system, ticketing) automatically
- it needs a **custom connector, MCP server or API integration**
- it must **run on its own** on a schedule or trigger, or take actions without a person in the loop (agentic automation)
- it must handle **high volume reliably**, with monitoring, security review and an owner on call
- it handles **regulated or sensitive data** in a way your approved tools don't cover

At that point, your prototype is still valuable. It is the clearest possible specification. Hand over the Artifact, the requirements, real test examples (including the ones that failed), and what users said. That makes the technical team's job far easier.

## Worked example

A marketing coordinator, Lena, wants a better way to brief the design team.

- **Design**: she asks Claude for three possible brief formats. She picks a one-page structured brief.
- **Build**: Claude creates it as an interactive Artifact. It's a form that asks campaign questions and produces a tidy brief at the end.
- **Test**: two designers and two marketers try it on last month's real campaigns. Feedback: the form never asks about deadlines, and the brand-colour field confuses people.
- **Iterate**: Lena asks for exactly those two changes and nothing else. The second round of testing passes.
- **Boundary**: her manager asks whether the form could create tickets in the design team's project-management tool automatically. Lena recognizes that needs an integration and sends the prototype, plus the requirement, to the internal developer team.

## What the exam looks for

Strong answers **prototype quickly, test with real users and examples, iterate with specific feedback, and escalate technical builds**. Weak answers try to make Claude do production engineering from a chat window, regenerate from scratch after every comment, or skip testing because the first draft "looks good".
keyTakeaways: Use Artifacts and file creation to make concrete prototypes (documents, decks, forms, dashboards, small tools) that people can react to.
Projects package a reusable assistant; Skills package a repeatable method where allowed.
Define success before building, test with real examples (including awkward ones), and iterate with targeted change requests.
Ask Claude for several design options early; changing direction late costs more.
Live system integrations, connectors or MCP servers, scheduled or autonomous automation and high-volume production use go to Developers or Architects.
A tested prototype plus examples and feedback makes the best hand-off specification.
examTips: If a scenario wants something reusable and shareable, an Artifact (or a Project for a recurring assistant) usually beats a long inline chat answer.
When feedback arrives, pick the option that asks for specific changes while keeping what works, not "regenerate from scratch".
Any requirement to connect automatically to company systems or run unattended signals escalation to a Developer or Architect.
Escalating does not mean discarding the prototype: options that hand it over with requirements and test cases are strongest.
commonTraps: Treating a working chat prototype as production-ready.
Trying to build integrations or automated actions as an Associate instead of escalating.
Testing only on the easy example Claude was shown while building.
Changing many things at once so you cannot tell which change fixed or broke something.

lessons.title: Integrating Claude into existing workflows: augment or redesign
lessons.eli5: You can give a bakery a faster mixer (augment) or rethink the whole kitchen around the new mixer (redesign). Either way, someone still tastes the bread before it goes on the shelf, and the head baker stays in charge.
lessons.body:
## Two ways to bring Claude in

Task 4.4 asks you to **fit Claude into work that already exists**. There are two broad options, and the exam expects you to know when each one fits.

| | Augment | Redesign |
|---|---|---|
| What changes | Claude takes over or speeds up **one step** | The **sequence of steps** is rethought around what Claude makes cheap |
| Example | Claude drafts the weekly status report; the manager edits and sends it | Status reports are replaced by a shared Project where anyone can ask for the current state, and the weekly meeting shrinks to decisions only |
| Risk | Low: the surrounding process and owners stay the same | Higher: roles, checks and hand-offs change |
| Effort | Small, quick to try | Needs stakeholder buy-in, testing and change management |
| Best when | You're starting out, or the process works and just has slow steps | The process exists mainly because a step used to be expensive (reading, drafting, summarizing) |

A sensible path is **augment first, then redesign** once you have evidence. Augmenting one step teaches you where Claude is reliable in your context, and that evidence justifies a bigger change.

## Where Claude usually fits inside a workflow

- **Intake**: summarizing incoming requests, sorting them by type or urgency, pulling out key details.
- **Drafting**: first versions of standard documents, replies, reports and proposals.
- **Review support**: checking a draft against a checklist or style guide and flagging gaps.
- **Knowledge lookup**: a Project loaded with policies or product documents that answers team questions.
- **Synthesis**: turning many inputs (feedback, notes, survey answers) into themes and recommendations.

Connectors (for example Google Drive, Gmail and Calendar, where your organization enables them) let Claude read context from tools you already use, so you aren't copying and pasting. They are configured by your plan and admins. You use what's approved; you don't bolt on unapproved tools.

## Keep humans at the costly points

Whichever path you take, **put a human checkpoint wherever an error would be expensive**: anything sent to customers, regulators or the public, anything with legal, financial or medical weight, and any decision about a person (hiring, performance, eligibility). Name an **owner** for each checkpoint. "Someone will look at it" isn't a control.

Augmenting judgment differs from replacing it. Claude can draft the rejection letter; a person decides the application is rejected.

Avoid the **rubber-stamp trap**: once outputs look good for a few weeks, reviewers start approving without reading. Keep reviews meaningful with spot-check samples, a short checklist, and by tracking how often reviewers make corrections.

## Measure before and after

You can't show a workflow improved unless you measured it first. Capture a baseline, then compare.

| Measure | Example |
|---|---|
| Time per item | Minutes to produce one client summary |
| Throughput | Requests handled per week |
| Quality | Errors found in review, rework rate, checklist pass rate |
| Consistency | Variation between team members' outputs |
| Experience | Staff and customer satisfaction |

If quality drops while speed rises, the change isn't finished. Adjust the prompt, the instructions or the checkpoint before scaling.

## Worked example

A customer-success team writes quarterly business reviews (QBRs) for 40 clients. Each one takes an account manager about four hours.

**Augment (month 1).** The team builds a Project with the QBR template, writing guidelines and example reviews. Account managers attach each client's usage export and meeting notes. Claude drafts the review, the account manager verifies every number against the source report and edits the narrative. Time drops to about ninety minutes. Review finds two number errors in the first ten drafts, so the instructions are updated to quote figures only from the attached export and to flag anything it can't find.

**Redesign (quarter 2).** With evidence in hand, the team rethinks the process. Claude produces a first-pass health summary for every account at the start of the quarter, and managers spend the saved time on the at-risk accounts instead of formatting slides. The checkpoint stays: every number is verified, and the account manager signs off before anything reaches the client. Pulling usage data automatically from the analytics platform is raised with the internal developer team as a separate request.

## What the exam looks for

The best answers **start small, keep human checkpoints where errors are costly, measure the result and stay within approved tools**. Distractors remove the human from high-stakes steps, redesign everything at once without evidence, or measure nothing.
keyTakeaways: Augment = Claude improves one step in an unchanged process; redesign = the process itself is rethought around what Claude makes cheap.
Augment first to build evidence, then redesign where that evidence supports it.
Common fits: intake, drafting, review support, knowledge lookup and synthesis.
Put a named human checkpoint wherever errors are costly: external audiences, legal, financial or medical content, and decisions about people.
Guard against rubber-stamp reviews with checklists, spot checks and tracked correction rates.
Measure a baseline (time, throughput, quality, consistency, satisfaction) and compare after the change.
examTips: For a first integration, choose the option that augments one well-defined step with a human review over one that automates the whole process at once.
If an option removes human sign-off on customer-facing or high-stakes output, eliminate it.
Options that define success metrics and a baseline before rollout beat ones that "roll out and see".
Connectors and integrations should be the approved ones; answers that bypass IT or policy for convenience are wrong.
commonTraps: Equating "integrate Claude" with "remove the human" from the process.
Redesigning an entire workflow on day one, with no evidence that Claude is reliable for that work.
Keeping a review step on paper while reviewers approve without reading.
Claiming success from speed alone while error rates quietly rise.

lessons.title: Communicating Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
lessons.eli5: When you tell your boss about a new tool, you show what it really did (saved two hours a week) and you're honest about what it can't do (it sometimes makes up facts, so someone checks its work). Honest promises are the ones people keep trusting.
lessons.body:
## The job

Task 4.5 is about being the **honest translator** between what Claude can do and what stakeholders (your manager, executives, clients, legal or IT, colleagues) expect. Over-selling causes as much damage as under-selling. If you promise "fully automated" and the first error reaches a client, trust in the whole program collapses.

## Talk about value in business terms

Stakeholders care about outcomes, not features. Translate.

| Instead of | Say |
|---|---|
| "Claude has Projects and Artifacts" | "Our proposal drafts now take 2 hours instead of 6, and the format is consistent across the team" |
| "It's a very capable model" | "In a 4-week pilot, 85% of drafts needed only light edits" |
| "AI will transform our process" | "We freed about a day a week for each analyst, which we moved to client calls" |

The common value themes are **time saved, capacity freed, consistency, quality of first drafts, speed of response, and coverage** (reading more material than a person could). Back each one with **evidence from a pilot**, not vendor claims or a single impressive demo.

## Be candid about limitations

State limitations plainly and pair each one with how you're handling it:

| Limitation | What to tell stakeholders | Control |
|---|---|---|
| Can produce confident but wrong details (hallucinations) | "It can invent plausible-sounding facts, figures or citations" | Key facts are verified against sources; human review before external use |
| Knowledge has a training cutoff | "It may not know recent events unless it searches or we give it current documents" | Use web search or Research, or supply current files |
| Works only from what it can see | "It doesn't know our internal context unless we provide it" | Projects with maintained knowledge files, approved connectors |
| Long conversations degrade | "Very long threads can lose earlier details" | Fresh chats with summaries; durable context in Projects |
| Output varies between runs | "The same request can give different wording" | Templates, instructions and review checklists |
| Data handling rules apply | "Only approved data goes into approved tools" | Follow the organization's AI and data policies |
| Accountability can't be delegated | "A person is responsible for anything we send" | Named owners and sign-off steps |

The Help Center itself says Claude can sometimes give incorrect or misleading responses and that important information should be checked. Quoting this to stakeholders builds credibility rather than undermining the project.

## Tailor the message to the audience

- **Executives**: outcome, evidence, risk, cost of the next step, the decision you need. One page.
- **Team members**: what changes in their day, what stays their responsibility, how to raise problems. Address the fear of replacement honestly. The usual story is augmentation (Claude takes the tedious drafting, people keep the judgment) where that's true.
- **Legal, compliance, IT**: what data goes in, which approved tools are used, where humans review, how outputs are logged or retained under policy.
- **Clients**: be transparent about AI assistance wherever your policy or contract expects it, and stress that a qualified person reviews the work.

Claude can help prepare all of these. Ask it to draft the executive summary from your pilot data, or to anticipate objections ("list the ten hardest questions a skeptical CFO would ask about this pilot"). Check every number in the draft yourself.

## Setting expectations that last

1. **Promise a pilot, not a transformation.** Small scope, clear metrics, a review date.
2. **Name what stays human**: approvals, decisions about people, final sign-off.
3. **Report problems openly**, including the errors the review step caught. That is evidence the controls work.
4. **Flag what needs other roles**: if stakeholders want automatic system integrations or autonomous agents, say plainly that this needs a Developer or Architect and a proper build, not a bigger prompt.

## Worked example

A finance operations analyst, Marcus, piloted Claude for drafting monthly variance commentary. His update to the CFO:

> **Result:** Over 3 month-ends, first drafts took 25 minutes instead of 2 hours. Reviewers rated 80% of drafts as needing only minor edits.
> **Limits we found:** Twice, Claude described a variance with the wrong cause when the source data didn't explain it. Our reviewer caught both. Commentary now cites only causes listed in the controller's notes, and says "cause not provided" otherwise.
> **Controls:** Every figure is checked against the ledger export; the controller signs off before distribution.
> **Ask:** Extend to two more business units for one quarter. Pulling data straight from the ledger system would need the internal developer team and is not part of this request.

This is credible because it is specific, shows the failures alongside the wins, and asks for a measured next step.

## What the exam looks for

The best answer **pairs evidence-based value with candid limits and clear human accountability**. Distractors overpromise ("fully automated", "eliminates errors"), hide limitations to win approval, or are so negative they stop useful, controllable work.
keyTakeaways: Frame value in business outcomes (time, capacity, consistency, quality, speed) backed by pilot evidence, not features or demos.
State limitations plainly (hallucinations, knowledge cutoff, missing internal context, long-thread drift, run-to-run variation, data rules) and pair each with a control.
Accountability stays with people: name who reviews and signs off.
Tailor the message: executives want outcome, evidence, risk and the decision; teams want what changes and what stays theirs; legal and IT want data flows and controls.
Promise a scoped pilot with metrics, report caught errors openly, and flag work that needs Developers or Architects.
examTips: Eliminate any option that promises full automation, zero errors or no need for review.
Prefer answers that cite pilot data and disclose limitations together over answers that only highlight benefits.
When a stakeholder asks for integrations or autonomous agents, the right response names the escalation path rather than promising it from a chat tool.
For worried team members, the best answer is honest about what changes and what stays their responsibility, not a blanket reassurance.
commonTraps: Using one impressive demo as proof of reliability.
Hiding errors found during the pilot to make the case look stronger.
Being so cautious that you recommend not using Claude at all, when controls would make the work safe.
Saying "Claude is responsible for the content" instead of naming a human owner.

lessons.title: Running a Claude pilot: scope, metrics and go/no-go
lessons.eli5: Before a café changes its whole menu, it runs a new dish as a "special" for two weeks and counts how many people order it and send it back. A pilot is the same: try Claude on one job, keep score, then decide.
lessons.body:
## Why a pilot ties the domain together

A pilot is where tasks 4.1 to 4.5 meet. You **chose a use case** (4.1), **planned** it (4.2), **built and iterated** a solution (4.3), **fitted it into the workflow** (4.4), and now you need **evidence to communicate** (4.5). Many exam scenarios are really asking: what is the sensible, measurable next step?

## Pilot design in six decisions

| Decision | Good choice | Weak choice |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | One task, one team, a fixed period (for example 4 to 6 weeks) | "Roll it out to everyone and see" |
| Baseline | Measure the current time, error rate and volume before starting | No baseline, so improvement is guesswork |
| Success criteria | Agreed in advance ("drafts in under 30 minutes, no more errors than today") | Decided after seeing the results |
| Test material | Real, representative cases, including difficult ones | Only the easy examples used to build the prompt |
| Controls | Named reviewer, checklist, approved tools and data only | Review "when there's time" |
| Feedback | Short log of corrections and user comments | Anecdotes collected at the end |

## What to measure

Keep it simple: one or two numbers per category.

- **Efficiency**: time per item, items per week.
- **Quality**: corrections per draft, errors caught in review, errors that escaped review.
- **Adoption**: how many people actually use it, and for what.
- **Experience**: a quick rating from the people doing the work and, where relevant, the people receiving it.

**Errors that escaped review** is the most important number. It tells you whether the human checkpoint works.

## Use Claude to run the pilot, carefully

Claude can help: draft the pilot plan and success criteria, design a feedback form as an Artifact, summarize the correction log into themes, and draft the end-of-pilot report. Two cautions:
- Recalculate any totals or percentages Claude reports from your data, or have it show the working.
- Give it the real log; don't let it fill gaps with plausible numbers.

## Making the call

At the end, choose one of four outcomes and say why:

1. **Scale**: criteria met and controls held. Extend to more teams, keeping the checkpoint.
2. **Adjust and re-run**: promising but quality is off. Improve instructions, knowledge files or the review checklist, then test again.
3. **Escalate**: value is clear but needs integration, automation or volume beyond chat tools. Hand to Developers or Architects with the evidence.
4. **Stop**: the task turned out to be a poor fit (errors are hard to catch, or the savings are tiny). Stopping a pilot is a valid, useful result.

## Worked example

A legal-operations coordinator pilots Claude for summarizing incoming supplier contracts for the procurement team (not for giving legal advice). Baseline: 45 minutes per summary. Success criteria: under 15 minutes, and every summary matching a lawyer's spot check on key dates and renewal terms. After five weeks, summaries take 12 minutes, but the spot check finds two missed auto-renewal clauses in 60 contracts. Decision: **adjust and re-run**. The instructions now require a dedicated "renewal and termination" section that quotes the clause or says "not found", and lawyers check every renewal section for the next round. The report to the head of legal shows both the time saved and the misses, and how they were fixed.

## What the exam looks for

Prefer answers that **scope small, measure against a baseline, agree criteria in advance and keep human checkpoints**. Be wary of answers that scale before evidence exists, or that judge success on speed alone.
keyTakeaways: A good pilot has a narrow scope, a baseline, success criteria agreed in advance, realistic test cases, named controls and a feedback log.
Measure efficiency, quality, adoption and experience; "errors that escaped review" shows whether the checkpoint works.
Claude can draft the plan, forms and report, but recalculate its numbers and give it the real log.
End with a clear decision: scale, adjust and re-run, escalate, or stop. Stopping is a valid result.
examTips: If asked for the best next step after a promising but imperfect pilot, choose "adjust and re-test" over "scale now" or "abandon".
Options that set success criteria before the pilot beat options that define success afterwards.
If the pilot proves value but needs system integration, the answer is to escalate with evidence.
commonTraps: Running a pilot with no baseline, so no improvement can be shown.
Testing only with the examples used to build the prompt.
Scaling on speed gains while quality metrics are missing or worsening.

lessons.title: Workflow drill: pick the measured, human-checked path
lessons.eli5: Most workflow questions have one answer that rushes, one that gives up, one that uses the wrong tool, and one that takes a sensible small step with someone checking the work. Learn to spot that last one.
lessons.body:
## The pattern behind domain 4 questions

Workflow questions describe a workplace situation and ask what you should do next. The four options usually include:

| Option type | What it looks like | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Overreach** | Automate the whole process, remove review, promise full automation, build integrations yourself | Wrong |
| **Abandon** | Stop using Claude, do everything manually, refuse because AI "can't be trusted" | Usually wrong when a safe path exists |
| **Wrong tool or wrong level** | Switch platforms, pick a feature that doesn't fit, rewrite the prompt when the real need is an integration | Wrong |
| **Measured step** | Use Claude for the part it's good at, keep a named human checkpoint, verify proportionally, measure, escalate technical work | Usually right |

## A five-question filter

Run each option through these:

1. **Does a human keep the decision** where errors are costly (external audiences, regulated content, decisions about people)?
2. **Is it proportionate?** Start small, gather evidence, then scale.
3. **Is it the right feature?** Chat for quick work, a Project for recurring work with shared instructions and files, Research for cited multi-source investigation, an Artifact for shareable output.
4. **Does it stay inside the Associate role?** Integrations, custom connectors or MCP servers, and autonomous agents go to Developers or Architects.
5. **Is it honest?** No overpromising to stakeholders; limitations are disclosed with controls.

## Practice scenarios (original)

**1. The vague mandate.** Your director says "find ways to use Claude in procurement". What first?
- Strong: gather the procurement team's current tasks and pain points, have Claude organize and score candidate use cases (frequency, effort, error impact, data sensitivity, verifiability), then confirm the shortlist with the team.
- Weak: start automating purchase approvals because they take the longest.
*Why:* 4.1 rewards structured analysis and stakeholder validation. Approvals are judgment calls with financial impact.

**2. The cited briefing.** Research returned a well-cited report on competitor pricing that you'll present to the leadership team tomorrow.
- Strong: open and check the sources behind the key figures and claims before presenting, and flag single-source claims.
- Weak: present it as-is because every claim has a citation. Also weak: discard it and start over manually.
*Why:* 4.2 treats citations as checkable, not as proof. Verify in proportion to the audience.

**3. The prototype request.** A team lead loves your interactive intake-form Artifact and asks you to make it create tickets in the service-desk system automatically.
- Strong: hand the prototype, requirements and test examples to the developer team for an integration build.
- Weak: try to make Claude update the system by pasting credentials into chat, or tell the lead it's impossible.
*Why:* 4.3 has a clear boundary, and the prototype becomes the specification.

**4. The first integration.** Recruiters want Claude to help with candidate screening.
- Strong: use Claude to summarize CVs against the published job criteria in an approved tool, with recruiters making every shortlisting decision and reviewing for bias.
- Weak: let Claude rank and reject candidates automatically to save time.
*Why:* 4.4 means augment, not replace, judgment, and decisions about people stay human.

**5. The executive update.** Your pilot cut report drafting time by 60%, and review caught three factual errors.
- Strong: report the time saving and the caught errors, explain the review step and fixes, and propose a scoped expansion.
- Weak: leave out the errors so approval is more likely, or claim the tool "eliminates manual work".
*Why:* 4.5 rewards evidence plus candor.

**6. The redesign temptation.** After two good weeks of Claude drafting customer replies with agent review, a manager proposes sending replies directly without review.
- Strong: keep review, gather more data (errors caught, escaped errors) and perhaps reduce review only for narrow, low-risk categories with spot checks, using policy and evidence.
- Weak: remove review now because the drafts "have been fine".
*Why:* two weeks isn't enough evidence, and the replies are customer-facing.

## Keywords that should catch your eye

- "**Fully**", "**always**", "**eliminate**", "**without review**" usually signal overreach.
- "**Pilot**", "**baseline**", "**validate with stakeholders**", "**verify the sources**", "**hand off to developers**" usually signal the measured step.
- A choice between **augment** and **redesign** with no evidence yet usually favors **augmenting first**.

## Final check

When two options both look reasonable, choose the one that **lets the work go ahead safely** over the one that blocks it, and the one that **fixes the real need** over the one that tweaks the prompt. If the real need is a system integration, no prompt will fix it.
keyTakeaways: Workflow distractors fall into overreach, abandonment and wrong-tool or wrong-level; the right answer is usually the measured, human-checked step.
Filter options by: human keeps costly decisions, proportionate scope, right feature, inside the Associate role, honest communication.
Words like "fully", "always", "eliminate" and "without review" usually signal a wrong option.
Augment first; redesign or reduce review only with evidence and within policy.
When the real need is an integration or automation, escalate to Developers or Architects with the prototype and requirements.
examTips: Eliminate overreach and abandonment options first, then choose between the remaining two by asking which one keeps a human at the costly point.
When the scenario mentions an external or senior audience, expect the right answer to include verification.
If the question asks for a "first step", pick discovery or analysis (map the process, gather requirements) over building.
Associate scenarios never expect you to write code or configure APIs; options that require it are usually the escalation cue.
commonTraps: Choosing the most impressive or most automated option because it saves the most time.
Choosing refusal because it feels safest, when an approved, reviewed path exists.
Fixing a prompt when the real gap is missing data access or a system integration.
Reducing human review on the strength of a few good results.
